title: A general, testable theory of asset prices under adaptive behavior

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a general theory explaining how asset prices form when market participants acquire information, learn from prices, compete with one another and adapt to available models. It would connect risk, information, liquidity and institutional constraints within a framework that produces distinctive predictions and states when those predictions should hold. This is a research objective, not an achieved capability.

A relevant foundation is Grossman and Stiglitz’s account of information acquisition and price informativeness as jointly determined. Investors’ incentives to obtain costly information depend on what prices already reveal, while the information investors obtain helps determine those prices. Their model therefore makes information and beliefs part of the price-formation process rather than treating them as fixed external inputs.

The broader proposed theory would explain whether and when discovering or publicizing a predictable pattern changes that pattern as participants respond. It would also identify circumstances in which observations cannot distinguish competing explanations. These are extensions to be developed and tested; the supplied paper does not establish adaptation to competing models or empirical changes in predictability following discovery.

significance.text: Conditional on achieving broad explanatory reach and prospective validation, the theory could provide finance with a more unified account of price formation across materially different markets. Its direct contribution would be to explain how interacting mechanisms generate prices and how those relationships change with conditions, while making explicit which explanations the evidence can distinguish. This is a reasoned assessment of the proposed capability’s significance, not a forecast of its success.

Grossman and Stiglitz supply a concrete reason such integration matters: information expenditure, differences in beliefs, risk preferences and price informativeness interact. A theory that treats these elements independently can miss the feedback between what participants learn and their incentive to keep learning. Extending that reasoning to liquidity, institutions and adaptation across markets remains part of the proposed advance.

Potential applications include better distinguishing compensation for bearing risk from mispricing, evaluating portfolio choices and assessing financial policy. Each would require separate evidence and adequate identification. Even a successful theory need not uniquely explain every price movement, deliver reliable excess returns or improve policy outcomes automatically. Its foundational value would lie in explanatory breadth and testable limits; profitable trading alone would not establish that value.

missing_breakthrough.text: The central missing capability, as defined by this proposal, is a tractable theory that derives falsifiable predictions while allowing participants’ learning and competition to alter the relationships being predicted. It must specify which responses follow from its mechanisms, which depend on market conditions and what observations would count against it. Simply adjusting a model after each market change would not meet this objective.

One concrete theoretical barrier is maintaining consistency between information incentives and informative prices. Grossman and Stiglitz show the tension that arises when acquiring information is costly but perfectly informative prices would remove the private return needed to motivate that acquisition. A broader theory must account for this feedback while extending beyond the assumptions of their detailed example.

Identification is a separate barrier. Within the supplied model, participants cannot fully separate information from supply shocks by observing prices. That illustrates limited inference within a specified model; it does not establish that financial theories are generally observationally equivalent. The proposed breakthrough must determine when risk compensation, information effects, liquidity pressures and institutional constraints can be distinguished, and when the available observations leave multiple explanations viable.

As a synthesis of the research objective, further engineering challenges include making learning rules and institutional assumptions explicit, connecting theoretical quantities to observable data, and producing uncertainty estimates that remain interpretable when conditions change. The theory would also need a disciplined way to delimit its scope rather than claiming generality through unrestricted flexibility.

current_state.text: Grossman and Stiglitz’s 1980 paper, “On the Impossibility of Informationally Efficient Markets,” establishes a theoretical constraint linking costly information acquisition to the informativeness of competitive prices. If prices reveal information so completely that acquiring it provides no private return, the incentive to pay for that information disappears. This is a model-based result, not an empirical demonstration that actual markets follow one general pricing theory.

The paper discusses learning the relationship between returns and prices and makes beliefs depend on information expenditure and price informativeness. Its detailed demonstration uses a particular example with constant absolute risk aversion and normally distributed quantities. Those assumptions delimit the demonstrated scope: the paper does not jointly resolve liquidity, institutional constraints, changing models and adaptive behavior across markets.

The supplied evidence does not establish whether a broader theory satisfying the proposed criteria existed as of November 1, 2026, the review’s stated freshness date. The search record was empty, and the reviewed evidence consists of the historical paper. Consequently, a categorical claim that all existing theories fall short would exceed this record. This gap leaves contemporary field-wide status unresolved without weakening the dated theoretical contribution.

The supplied review reports access to the complete 16-page article, pages 393–408, including appendices and references, without truncation. It also notes garbled mathematical extraction and uninspected figure details. The limited conclusions retained here rest on the reviewed prose and stated assumptions; the supplied review does not provide a basis for claiming independent verification of every derivation or figure.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: specify predictions, uncertainty, applicable conditions and failure conditions before observing the test outcomes. Predictions should differ meaningfully from those of competing explanations and be evaluated prospectively across selected asset classes, countries and market regimes. These are proposed evaluation criteria, not established standards prescribed by the supplied paper.
completion_criteria.label: Distinctive predictions specified before outcomes and tested prospectively

completion_criteria.text: Independent studies should reproduce central results and test the predicted mechanisms, including responses to natural or deliberate changes that affect information acquisition, competition or relevant constraints. For example, tests could examine whether a specified change in information costs alters acquisition incentives and price informativeness as predicted. Such a study would need to distinguish that mechanism from alternative causes of the observed price response.
completion_criteria.label: Independent studies reproduce central results and distinguish predicted mechanisms

completion_criteria.text: A convincing evidence package should report unsuccessful predictions, sensitivity to assumptions and cases in which observations fail to distinguish explanations. It should document enough about data, measurement and estimation for independent reproduction. Any claimed portfolio benefit should be tested separately under practical trading conditions; a winning backtest would not substitute for an explanatory test.
completion_criteria.label: Evidence reports explanatory failures and enables independent reproduction

completion_criteria.text: Completion would mean demonstrated explanatory breadth within clearly stated practical boundaries, including the tested markets, institutions, information conditions and regimes. Finite tests cannot establish literal universality. Evidence of success should therefore support a defined range of use and explicit limits, with broader applicability remaining open to further testing.
completion_criteria.label: Explanatory breadth demonstrated within tested conditions and explicit limits

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis: FIN-11, “Operational limits on the financial value of information and arbitrage,” is the closest overlap. FIN-01 concerns a broad explanation of asset prices under adaptive behavior; FIN-11 concerns a distinct quantitative limit on the value of information and arbitrage. A successful pricing theory might incorporate such a limit, but neither objective entails achievement of the other.

Roster-based synthesis: FIN-08, “A causal theory linking trading activity to market-wide liquidity crashes,” addresses a specific mechanism that could inform FIN-01’s treatment of liquidity. FIN-02, “Causal forecasting and prevention of systemic financial cascades,” concerns propagation and prevention of system-wide distress. Price formation, liquidity crashes and systemic cascades can interact, but their explanatory and intervention objectives remain distinct.

Roster-based synthesis: FIN-09, “Causal measurement of investment’s financial and real-world impact,” shares the challenge of distinguishing causal explanations from associations. Explaining market prices would not by itself establish an investment’s real-world effects. FIN-03, “Run-resistant financing of long-lived, illiquid investment,” and FIN-10, “Scalable financing mechanisms for pure public goods,” concern financing arrangements whose incentives and constraints could become inputs to a pricing theory, while retaining separate design and performance goals.

Roster-based synthesis: FIN-04, “Low-cost, reliable insurance for previously uninsurable livelihoods,” and FIN-05, “Scalable financing for creditworthy people and firms without conventional credit histories,” involve risk and information problems relevant to financial valuation. FIN-06, “Universally accessible, near-instant cross-border money transfer,” and FIN-07, “Cash-like privacy and resilience for digital money,” concern payment and monetary infrastructure. These capabilities could change the environment in which prices form; a general pricing theory would not itself deliver their insurance, access, transfer, privacy or resilience outcomes.

change_log.reason: The supplied paper does not demonstrate empirical discovery effects or adaptation to competing models.

change_log.reason: One historical paper and an empty freshness record cannot establish the state of the entire field in 2026.

change_log.reason: The review supports a specific theoretical example and a model-specific identification problem, not unrestricted generality.

change_log.change: Separated conditional foundational significance from portfolio gains, policy benefits and unique attribution of price movements.
change_log.reason: Those downstream outcomes require additional evidence and identification.

change_log.change: Expanded the proposed validation approach to include independent reproduction, mechanism tests, failures, practical boundaries and limits on universality.
change_log.reason: These details operationalize explanatory generality without presenting proposed criteria as consensus standards.

change_log.reason: Readers need to understand the evidentiary scope and conceptual boundaries without merging distinct innovations.

unresolved_issues: Whether a broader theory meeting the proposed criteria existed as of November 1, 2026 remains unestablished by the supplied record.
The supplied evidence does not establish when discovery changes predictable market patterns or how participants adapt to competing models.
Which observations can distinguish risk compensation, mispricing, information effects, liquidity pressures and institutional constraints remains a central research question.
The feasibility and appropriate breadth of prospective cross-market mechanism tests remain unspecified; no numerical completion thresholds are established.
The review did not independently verify every mathematical derivation or figure because mathematical extraction was garbled and figure details were uninspected.

brief.title: An explanation of prices that change as traders learn
possible: Investors could better understand why prices move and when a familiar trading pattern should stop working as others discover it. A testable theory would connect how traders learn and compete with risk, ease of trading and the rules markets operate under.
why: Investors and policymakers would gain a shared explanation for price formation across different markets. It could help distinguish rewards for taking risk from mistaken pricing, and explain how changing access to information changes prices.

sources.who: Sanford J. Grossman and Joseph E. Stiglitz
sources.showed: Their model links the information prices reveal to investors’ incentives to buy information. Prices that reveal everything would remove the reward for paying to learn.
sources.quote:
We propose here a model in which there 
is an equilibrium degree of disequilibrium: 
prices reflect the information of informed 
individuals (arbitrageurs) but only partially, 
so that those who expend resources to ob- 
tain information do receive compensation.
sources.cited_for: Prices and incentives to acquire information must be explained together.
sources.not_established: The detailed result rests on restrictive assumptions and does not explain adaptation across different markets.

sources.who: R. David McLean and Jeffrey Pontiff
sources.showed: Trading strategies based on published stock-return patterns earned less after publication. The authors separated declines after the original study period from those following publication.
sources.quote: The average predictor’s long-short return shrinks 58% post-publication.
sources.cited_for: Publicizing a predictable pattern can be followed by a decline in its trading returns.
sources.not_established: Historical declines do not establish a general theory that predicts how traders will adapt.

sources.showed: Their international study found a reliable decline in trading-pattern returns after publication only in the United States. Differences persisted after accounting for how easily stocks could be traded.
sources.quote:
The same empirical framework shows that none 
of the 38 international markets in our sample yields a re- 
liable post-publication decline in anomaly returns.
sources.cited_for: Responses to published research differ across markets, so market conditions matter.
sources.not_established: The findings do not uniquely identify why markets respond differently or establish predictions made before outcomes.

sources.who: Charles G. McClure, Shawn X. Shi and Edward M. Watts
sources.showed: After countries introduced online systems for company disclosures, the researchers found less private information gathering and less information reflected in prices before earnings announcements.
sources.quote:
Our ﬁndings show that decreased information acquisition
costs through these technology adoptions reduce private information acquisition and
the informativeness of prices.
sources.cited_for: Easier access to public disclosures can weaken incentives to gather private information.
sources.not_established: This tests a particular information mechanism around earnings announcements, rather than a general explanation of prices.

shown: Grossman and Stiglitz established the core feedback in a mathematical model: prices reveal information, which changes the incentive to gather more. McLean and Pontiff found that published trading patterns weakened; Jacobs and Müller showed that this response differed across countries.
McClure, Shi and Watts linked easier access to company disclosures with less private information gathering. Together, these studies demonstrate pieces that a broader theory would need to explain.
missing: A theory must make predictions that traders’ learning can change, while stating clearly what outcomes would prove it wrong.
Tests must distinguish rewards for risk from pricing mistakes, information effects, trading difficulties and market rules.
The theory must connect its assumptions to measurable data and give meaningful uncertainty estimates as conditions change.

milestones.label: Distinctive predictions survive tests on future outcomes
milestones.explanation: Predictions, uncertainty and failure conditions would have to be set before tests across markets and conditions. This would distinguish the theory from explanations fitted after events.

milestones.label: Independent studies reproduce results and distinguish causes
milestones.explanation: Independent studies would have to reproduce central results and distinguish predicted causes when information costs, competition or constraints change. This would test whether the theory explains why prices respond.

milestones.label: Failures are reported and results can be reproduced
milestones.explanation: Studies would have to report failed predictions, dependence on assumptions and ambiguous explanations, with enough detail for reproduction. This would expose weaknesses; trading gains would require separate tests.

milestones.label: Broad explanatory success has clear boundaries
milestones.explanation: Tests would have to establish explanatory success across a defined range of markets and conditions, with explicit limits. This would establish where the theory works without claiming it explains every market.

uncertain: When does discovering a trading pattern change it, and how do traders respond to competing models?
Which observations can distinguish competing explanations for the same price movement?
How broad must tests across markets be to establish a general theory?

page.title: Asset pricing under adaptive learning
page.definition: A theory that derives asset prices when investors buy information, learn from prices, and change forecasting rules through learning and competition. It connects risk, trading costs and institutional constraints to predictions that observations can contradict.

goal.need: Publication-related changes in trading-pattern returns differ across markets. McLean and Pontiff studied 97 stock-return predictors from 79 studies and reported returns 26% lower after the original sample and 58% lower after publication. Jacobs and Müller examined 241 anomalies in the United States and 38 other markets; a robust publication-related decline appeared only in the United States. These findings motivate explaining when learning changes prices and when it does not.

statements.body: Economic Sciences Prize Committee, Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences
statements.quote: This year’s prize awards empirical work aimed at understanding how asset prices are determined.
statements.context: The scientific background document was published on 14 October 2013; its scope is asset pricing generally.

statements.body: Andrew W. Lo, developer of the Adaptive Markets Hypothesis
statements.quote: reconciles market efficiency with behavioral alternatives by applying the principles of evolution—competition, adaptation, and natural selection—to financial interactions.
statements.context: Lo states the purpose of his proposed framework.

completion.title: Independent evidence supports an asset-pricing model’s predictions about adaptive learning.
completion.criterion: A specified model jointly predicts asset prices and measured changes in investors’ information acquisition or forecasting rules. With its learning mechanism and institutional assumptions fixed, its predictions distinguish it from specified risk-only and non-adaptive alternatives on data excluded from model construction. An independent study reproduces that discrimination within the stated domain. Rejection conditions are specified. No common numerical accuracy, market-count or replication threshold was found.
completion.set_by: Atlas fallback; no external completion criterion identified.
completion.basis: Searched the Academy’s 2013 assessment, Lo’s 2004 framework, the OECD’s 2020 discussion, the accessible 2024 Lo–Zhang book description, and searches for adaptive-market standards, prize rules and validation benchmarks. No general acceptance test was found. This narrow fallback requires independently supported predictions about both prices and adaptation, the capability described by the goal statements.

milestones.title: A pricing model proves an equilibrium with an informed-investor fraction strictly between zero and one.
milestones.criterion: Prove existence of a market-clearing price function and an informed-investor fraction λ with 0 < λ < 1, such that buying costly information and remaining uninformed yield equal ex ante expected utility. Grossman and Stiglitz’s Theorem 3 establishes this for their Gaussian, constant-absolute-risk-aversion model when γ(0) < 1 < γ(1), where γ is the ratio of informed to uninformed expected utility. This establishes consistency of information incentives and prices within those assumptions.
milestones.set_by: Grossman and Stiglitz, American Economic Review (1980), sections I.E–F; model-specific equilibrium definition and peer-reviewed proof.
milestones.threshold_quote: the expected utility of the informed is equal to that of the uninformed

milestones.title: A laboratory test rejects full revelation’s one-third share of purchases by type-I traders.
milestones.criterion: In Copeland and Friedman’s design, type-I traders have the highest good-state dividend. Compare their share of information purchases with forecasts of 1/3 under full revelation and 2/3 under nonrevelation using the published z-test. Reject full revelation while retaining nonrevelation in the heterogeneous-payoff treatment. Their 1992 paper reports eight experiments with nine traders each; in later heterogeneous-treatment periods, 62 of 96 purchases were by type-I traders, with z = 3.75 and −0.25 respectively.
milestones.set_by: Copeland and Friedman, Journal of Business (1992), section IV.E; published experimental protocol for this laboratory design.
milestones.threshold_quote: the FRE and PI forecasts are convincingly rejected

milestones.title: Stock-return predictor portfolios show a publication-related decline significant at the 5% level.
milestones.criterion: In McLean and Pontiff’s panel design, estimate separate post-sample and post-publication effects on monthly long–short predictor returns, controlling for time effects. Obtain a negative post-publication coefficient significant at the paper’s 5% level. Their 2016 paper studies 97 predictors from 79 studies through 2013; with time fixed effects, returns were 31.0 basis points per month lower post-publication. Jacobs and Müller’s 2020 international extension finds a robust decline only in the United States.
milestones.set_by: McLean and Pontiff, Journal of Finance (2016), Table III and section III.D; significance criterion used in this published empirical test.

milestones.title: Disclosure-system adoption changes pre-announcement price informativeness at the 1% significance level.
milestones.criterion: Use McClure, Shi and Watts’s staggered-adoption design: the post-adoption coefficient on the price-jump ratio is positive and significant at 1%. This ratio divides announcement-window returns (days −1 to +2) by returns over days −21 to +2. An increase indicates less information incorporated before earnings announcements. Published on 22 July 2025, the paper reports this across specifications for 23,354 firms and 239,971 firm-years during 1992–2017 in 32 countries, subject to its identification assumptions.
milestones.set_by: McClure, Shi and Watts, Review of Accounting Studies (2025), section 5.1 and Table 4; significance criterion used in this disclosure-technology test.
milestones.threshold_quote: is positive across all specifications and is statistically significant at the 1% level.

milestones.title: An adaptive pricing model distinguishes its predictions from alternatives on previously unused market data.
milestones.criterion: A specified model jointly predicts prices and observed information acquisition or forecasting-rule changes on market data excluded from its construction. Its predictions discriminate it from specified risk-only and non-adaptive alternatives under an announced decision rule, within explicit institutional conditions. This is the initial successful test preceding independent confirmation. The cited studies establish separate information and publication effects; no integrated result meeting this test was identified.
milestones.set_by: Atlas fallback; searches of adaptive-market frameworks and validation benchmarks found no externally prescribed integrated predictive milestone.

not_found: No society, agency, prize or roadmap criterion for completion of a general adaptive asset-pricing theory was found.
No externally prescribed integrated predictive milestone linking prices and observed adaptive behaviour was found.
The full text of Lo and Zhang’s 2024 book was access restricted; its publisher’s abstract and contents were available.
No opened source established that a single adaptive model satisfies the completion test.

results.finding: In a theoretical model with no empirical sample, the equilibrium informed fraction is strictly between 0 and 1.
results.detail: Under the Gaussian, constant-absolute-risk-aversion assumptions, the interior equilibrium holds when γ(0) < 1 < γ(1); informed and uninformed expected utilities are equal.

results.finding: Across 97 predictor portfolios, monthly returns were 31.0 basis points lower post-publication with time fixed effects.
results.detail: The panel separately estimates post-sample and post-publication effects; the post-publication decline is significant at the 5% level.
results.quote:
In particular, predictor
returns are 17.9 bps lower out-of-sample and 31.0 bps lower post-publication,

results.finding: US predictor portfolios: 99,214 anomaly-months; baseline post-publication returns fell 45 basis points per month.
results.detail: The study estimates separate post-sample and post-publication effects. The US post-publication effect remains significant with month fixed effects; the 45-basis-point estimate is from the baseline specification.

results.finding: A pricing model with N ≥ 3 investor types proves an equilibrium with 0 < λN < 1.
results.detail: In a symmetric economy under the stated cost conditions, Proposition 6.9 establishes an interior equilibrium. Proposition 3.2 supplies the market-clearing price function, and the equilibrium condition requires equal ex ante expected utility for informed and uninformed type-N agents.
